https://www.politico.eu/article/climate-.text: Climate and artificial intelligence are set to feature prominently in Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union address, according to two officials. Bjoern Seibert, the European Commission president's powerful head of cabinet, discussed the likely themes of the speech with the other 26 commissioners’ chiefs of staff at their traditional post-summer meeting on Friday, held this year in Jodoigne, Wallonia. The gathering included a session dedicated to the Commission president's Sept. 16 address, which is currently being drafted, where cabinet heads pitched Seibert their departments' priorities for inclusion in the speech. Advertisement Advertisement During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks. The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition. The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials. Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta , according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said. The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized. The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover. Advertisement Advertisement For commissioners, even a fleeting reference in the State of the Union matters. A line in the speech can propel a policy file up the executive’s political pecking order, giving cabinets every incentive to fight for space. But with limited room in one of Brussels’ most closely watched speeches, not everyone will make the cut. Commissioners will get another opportunity to lobby von der Leyen when they gather for the traditional College seminar in Tervuren next week, marking the start of the new political season. "It will be the last chance for commissioners to catch her eye before the speech," said one of the officials. The Commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text: Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, at inspects his burnt-out warehouse. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, at inspects his burnt-out warehouse. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian The Sunday read Ukraine Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books A Ukrainian publishing boom sparked by the 2022 invasion is now under threat from the force and frequency of Russian attacks Charlotte Higgins in Kharkiv, Kremenchuk, Kyiv and Lviv. Photographs by Julia Kochetova Sun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 03.31 EDT Share On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves. Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.” View image in fullscreen Eight million books were destroyed in the drone strike and subsequent fire at Ranok’s warehouse in Kharkiv. The meeting was scheduled for 11am. But a couple of moments after it began, there came “the sound of an explosion, and almost simultaneously I saw a huge fire”, said Kruglov. The impact was about 30 metres from where the staff were gathered, and, as colleagues set about trying to put out the flames, “there came a second strike and I understood that there could be a third, and a fourth, so we started to evacuate”. The munitions used in the attack were jet-powered Shaheds, a recent and insidious escalation of Russian drone technology, faster and harder to intercept than their predecessors. These are the weapons that have been lately terrorising Kyiv during daylight hours, ploughing into the National Academy of Sciences and a working medical clinic in the past week. “Fifty people were on shift that day,” said Kruglov of the warehouse strike, “and I don’t know how to explain how nobody was injured.” The combination of an explosion, jet fuel and a warehouse full of paper was catastrophic. None of the books could be salvaged and 8m were destroyed. It took firefighters a week to bring the flames under control. View image in fullscreen The burnt remains of sheet music at Ranok’s warehouse, which was destroyed in an attack using jet-powered Shaheds. Several weeks on, smoke still rose from parts of the warehouse. The roof seemed on the verge of collapse, metal beams listing alarmingly, twisted out of shape by the heat. Shafts of sunlight slanted through the damaged roof, illuminating the catastrophe. The smell was terrible, clinging to clothes and hair. As far as the eye could see, the wreckage of books lay in mounds. In some places, engulfed by the firefighters’ water, they had dissolved into a thick, stinking, mud-like slurry. In others, they were charred at the edges but recognisable as what they once were: children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers, geography textbooks, young-adult fiction. Others were nothing but swollen millefeuilles of blackened pages that flaked away to the touch. View image in fullscreen Children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers were among the books destroyed or damaged. A couple of editorial staff, visiting the wreckage for the first time since the attack, looked shaken as they recognised fragments of books they had written or edited. “When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it’s an awful feeling,” said Kruglov, a trim, bald, blue-eyed man in his early 60s. Those 8m books represented more than 85% of Ranok’s total stock, he said. In the main branch of Ranok’s own Knyholand bookstore in Kyiv, the display still looked cheerful and dense in late September – but, predicted Kruglov, there will be shortages this autumn when the books instore run low and there is nothing to replace them. In total, this summer, 13m Ukrainian books have been destroyed by Russian missiles or drones – a third, estimates the government, of all books printed in Ukraine this year. Books, literature, culture and language are not peripheral to Russia’s war on Ukraine – they are bound up in it. The full-scale invasion in February 2022 was prompted, at least in part, by Vladimir Putin’s conviction that Ukraine and Russia have no true separate cultural identity. Kruglov said he was sure his warehouse full of Ukrainian-language, Ukraine-produced books had been deliberately targeted. “It is nowhere near any military facilities and everyone knows it is a book warehouse,” he said. Bohdana Laiuk, a Ukrainian deputy minister for culture, who works on literature and publishing, takes a slightly different view: the recent attacks on books should not be seen in isolation, but as part of the invaders’ recent campaign of attacking warehouses, depots and fulfilment centres of any kind. “They cannot occupy Kyiv,” she said. “So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us – and books are part of everyday life.” View image in fullscreen The books destroyed in the Kharkiv attack represented 85% of Ranok’s total stock, according to the CEO of the publisher. But books are also part of language, and language is part of identity and, often, nationhood. Books are, said Laiuk, certainly considered important by the Russians invaders. “When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do – and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions – is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them,” she said. Until 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market was Russian-language titles – most imported from Russia, some published in Ukraine. The dominance of Russian publishing had a long history. Its seeds lay in 19th-century decrees under the tsars against publishing in Ukrainian and continued through the Soviets’ promotion of Russian as the language of aspiration, education and culture. Ukrainian writers were purged and Ukrainian literature left in the shadows, shut out from a canon that lionised the Russian novel. After Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the idea of a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel that tackled modern social issues was so unthinkable that publishers initially suggested to Oksana Zabuzhko that her 1996 novel Fieldwork in Ukrainian Sex be published in Russian translation. She insisted it was published in the language it was written. It became a bestseller, paving the road for waves of contemporary Ukrainian literature. View image in fullscreen Bohdana Laiuk: ‘When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do … is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books and destroy them.’ Laiuk characterised the dominance of Russian book imports as a kind of colonialism. “It should be compared to how Russians invested in Ukrainian media outlets, Ukrainian TV channels, Ukrainian newspapers and magazines.” It was a conscious policy, she argued. “This is how Russians think: when they arrive on tanks, everything will be ready for them because they already have this information space.” But in 2022, Ukrainian booksellers abruptly stopped selling Russian imports, in line with the rupture of all commercial ties between the countries. At the same time, swathes of the Ukrainian population switched their day-to-day language from Russian to Ukrainian. They switched reading matter, too, and Ukraine’s publishers fed the appetite with new editions of classic Ukrainian literature from the 1920s, poetry, translations, and new Ukrainian writing. The country’s publishers may publish Russian-language books, as long as at least half their titles are in Ukrainian; in practice the social barriers to doing so, at the moment, would be prohibitive. (Death and the Penguin author Andrey Kurkov, for example, writes his novels in Russian, but they are published only in Ukrainian translation; he writes nonfiction and children’s books in Ukrainian.) “People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Laiuk told me in 2023 . “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.” View image in fullscreen Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. In 2024, while the city was under fire, he opened a second, in a huge building on Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s grandest boulevard, to which he has recently added a third floor, with an expansive events space. He has another branch in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk and he has just opened a fourth, in a former cinema in Lviv. “When you go to a bookstore like Sens,” said Laiuk, “you feel that you have dignity. You have the right to buy a new book and to choose which one you like. And when you have drones above your head, it gives so much space, inner space in your heart and soul, and in your mind.” The rapid expansion of Sens is a symptom of something unlikely: a Ukrainian publishing boom amid a full-scale invasion of the country. And now, that boom is threatened by the force and frequency of Russian attacks. Kateryna and Artem Sova started their imprint in 2023, in the thick of the new Ukrainian publishing boom. By then Artem had been in the army for nearly a year and Kateryna was several months pregnant, living in her hometown of Kremenchuk, on the River Dnipro in central Ukraine. It was their dream: they had both worked in bookstores and at arts festivals for years. Part of the point for Artem was to keep some chink of his old self alive. “I realised,” he said, speaking in Zaporizhzhia during a break from his military duties, “that I was detached from everything I love.” View image in fullscreen Kateryna Sova said she and her husband, Artem, called their publishing house Krapky (Ellipsis) as they wanted reading their books ‘to be an ongoing conversation’. They began with Lonely City , a nonfiction work about art and the experience of urban isolation, by the British author Olivia Laing. They had loved it since they read it a decade ago, and were bemused it was not already translated. They wrote to Laing’s agent asking whether they could acquire the rights. “We tried to explain why this book is important for Ukrainians now, and to me personally,” Artem said, recalling. “This experience of being lonely is kind of universal, but it has been multiplied because a lot of people went into the army, and there are so many displaced people in Ukraine: separated couples, destroyed lives.” Laing, to their surprise, agreed: only then did they actually go through the legal process of setting up the company. They called it Krapky – Ukrainian for “ellipsis”, the three dots being their favourite punctuation mark, signifying, said Kateryna, as she sipped coffee in an independent bookshop in Kremenchuk, that they wanted reading their books “to be an ongoing conversation. Something that doesn’t stop when you close the book.” Their aim was for every book they published to be expertly translated and wonderfully illustrated. View image in fullscreen Part of the reason Artem Sova co-founded Krapky was to keep some chink of his old self alive while doing his military service. In 2025, they finally went to Kyiv Book Arsenal – the great annual gathering for publishers, writers and readers in the capital – with a beautifully designed edition of Lonely City. By this year’s Book Arsenal they had several titles already out, and translations of Laing’s To the River and Karen Blixen’s classic, Out of Africa, in the pipeline. In preparation were also works by Flannery O’Connor, among others. “We wanted to get to a position where we were publishing eight to 10 titles a year,” said Kateryna. Recently, they had signed a contract with Nova Poshta , the Ukrainian postal service, to handle fulfilment – so that Kateryna was not sending out the books herself to customers and bookstores. She was driving her sister to university on the morning of 28 August when Artem rang. The warehouse where their books were held, on the periphery of Kyiv, had been attacked. Kateryna had to pull off the road in her distress. At the Lviv BookForum, a fortnight later, their stand was empty but for a QR code so visitors could preorder their forthcoming titles. They had nothing physical to sell. All of their books had been destroyed. Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers, hoping to get precious teaching materials into schools – and plug the shortfall in cashflow with sales of popular titles. Vivat, a large Kharkiv-based publisher, which lost 16m Ukrainian hryvnia (about £270,000) worth of books in a hit on one of its warehouses this summer, is doing the same. “We’ll definitely continue publishing Ukrainian authors, and the schedule for 2027 is already finalised,” said Vivat’s spokesperson, Kateryna Ilchuk, between events at Lviv BookForum. “But probably yes, it will mean going with more mainstream titles.” View image in fullscreen Kateryna Sova shows the very last books that were left for sale after Russian attacks. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Small literary publishers such as Krapky are the most vulnerable in the current crisis. Another small independent press, Who is That?, recently announced a pause in its operations until the end of the war, after the destruction of all of their stock this summer in two separate airstrikes. For debut authors, or writers of less commercial or more experimental titles, this is a bleak moment. Even before the summer drone hits, there had been delays in some books’ publication owing to attacks on printing infrastructure. Ksenia Shpak’s debut young-adult novel – an urban fantasy about a girl internally displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathian mountains – was originally due out in February 2025. It was finally published, by the imprint Zhorzh, in November. But half the print run was in the Ranok warehouse in Kharkiv when it was attacked. “I must say that it’s sad because it was my first published book,” said Shpak, “and now my publisher will focus on their bestsellers, and only after that if they get enough money will they reprint my book.” She mentioned other factors that had lately cooled the Ukrainian publishing boom: a levelling out of demand; the rise in the cost of living. “It feels like there is a snowballing of bad things for our publishing industry,” Shpak added. View image in fullscreen For publishers such as Ivan Malkovych, the task now is to adapt: spread stocks of book in smaller warehouses across the country, at the expense of super-fast delivery times. “It’s shaky,” said veteran poetry editor, poet and children’s publisher Ivan Malkovych. His premises – in central Kyiv, shared with a male-voice choir, the sound of whose rehearsal wafted through the editorial offices as he spoke – presented an absolute contrast to the desolation of the Ranok warehouse. In one room, a wall of shelves displayed ranks of exquisitely illustrated children’s titles, and handsome volumes of poetry. https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2026/10/1.text: Oct. 12, 2026 Ukrainian service members launch a drone. REUTERS / Valentyn Ogirenko Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia on Monday of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, urging Washington to ensure Moscow abides by the agreement as the Kremlin said contacts over a possible truce were ongoing. Russia attacked gas production facilities belonging to Ukraine’s state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, causing a fire and damaging critical equipment, the company said Monday. Ukrainian drone attacks, meanwhile, appeared to spare Russian oil refineries overnight after Trump made the surprise announcement that the ceasefire had taken immediate effect. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday that contacts over a possible energy ceasefire were continuing. He declined to say whether it would apply only to oil refineries, saying further information would be released in due course. “There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump,” Zelensky told a security conference in Warsaw via video link. Zelensky said he had learned about the agreement through the media and was awaiting details of the terms discussed by Washington and Moscow. “This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it,” he said. The Kremlin has not formally confirmed that it agreed to a ceasefire. Sources close to the Russian government told Bloomberg that Moscow remained skeptical that Washington could deliver a binding agreement on terms favorable to Russia. news Trump Says Russia and Ukraine Reached ‘Energy Ceasefire' Read more Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said employees were working to repair the damage from the overnight attack. “Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” he said on Telegram. Zelensky also said in his nightly video address Sunday that Russian forces had struck a combined heat and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, that evening. A Ukrainian official said the attack took place after Trump’s ceasefire announcement. “The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky said in the address. Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 37 drones were destroyed as they approached the capital between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Local authorities and independent media reported no new strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has repeatedly targeted in recent months. Russian attacks on other targets continued Monday. The Defense Ministry said its forces struck a cargo vessel carrying military supplies near the Ukrainian port of Odesa. Local officials said Russian shelling and air attacks injured at least 12 people in Kharkiv that morning. In Russia’s southern Rostov region, firefighters continued battling a blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery following a drone attack Saturday, the exiled news outlet Astra reported . Authorities in the southwestern Belgorod region said one civilian was killed and three others were injured Sunday evening. Separately, Peskov rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire to allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections, saying Moscow wanted an overall peace deal instead. “Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday. Peskov said Putin and other Russian officials had repeatedly stated that they did not want a temporary ceasefire and were prepared to work toward long-term peace. Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelensky an illegitimate leader. Elections in wartime are prohibited by Ukrainian law. Reuters contributed reporting. https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/how-.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points A child under 18 usually joins a parent through a family permit tied to the parent's own status, or follows an EU-law track if a parent is an EU citizen; the child's documents must be ready before the application. Compulsory schooling in Czechia starts the school year after a child turns six, with a compulsory final pre-school year; enrolment for primary school takes place in spring (as of 2026; check the school and the district). Health insurance, address registration and the school place all need the child's permit or status, so the order of steps matters. On this page 6 sections The child's residence permit A child born in Czechia Health insurance before anything else Compulsory school Choosing between state and international schools After the permit: what to keep up Parents tend to plan a move around their own job and their own permit, and then discover that a seven-year-old has to be somewhere on 1 September. The Czech system treats the child as a separate applicant in three places at once: the Ministry of the Interior, the health insurer and the school. Knowing which order they must come in turns a chaotic spring into a manageable one. The Foreigners Act (Act No. 326/1999 Coll.) and the Education Act apply, and details change, so check each office's current instructions. The child's residence permit The route depends on the parent. If one parent is a Czech citizen, the child may be entitled to citizenship by descent; see our overview of how to apply for Czech citizenship for the general framework and ask the Ministry about the specific case. If a parent is an EU citizen living in Czechia, a non-EU child can obtain a residence card as a family member under EU law; see registration rules for EU citizens . If the parent holds a non-EU long-term or permanent residence permit, the child usually applies for a long-term permit for family reunification, which is the case this guide follows. How family reunification works in Czechia sets the wider context. The child must be a minor and unmarried, and the parent must meet the sponsor's conditions, including accommodation, means, health insurance and, as a general rule, 15 months of residence in Czechia before the family application; Blue Card, intra-company transfer and researcher permits are exempt and a shorter period is described for employee card holders (as of 2026; check MV/OAMP). Where only one parent lives in Czechia, the Ministry wants to see that the other parent agrees, or that the sponsoring parent has the right to decide where the child lives, usually through a court order or a consent document. Prepare it early, because it needs an apostille and a sworn translation. The usual documents are the child's passport, birth certificate, photographs, application form, proof of accommodation and insurance, and proof of the parent-child relationship. Young children are not fingerprinted; the Ministry's page gives the age limit. Foreign certificates follow the usual rule: apostille or legalisation, then sworn translation. See apostille and legalisation and sworn translations . A child born in Czechia A child born in Czechia to foreign parents does not automatically have a residence permit. The parents must apply to the Ministry of the Interior (OAMP) for the baby's residence within a period set in the Foreigners Act, commonly reported as 60 days from the birth (as of 2026; check MV for your case). Missing it creates avoidable trouble, so look it up in the first week. Register the birth first, get the Czech birth certificate, and then file with the Ministry. Our guide to the Czech birth number covers the number that the child receives. Health insurance before anything else A child needs health insurance from the day of arrival, and an application for a residence permit asks for proof. How the child is insured depends on the family's situation. If a parent works for a Czech employer and the child qualifies for the public system, the child is insured there; children are among the groups the state insures in certain situations, but for foreign children the conditions depend on their status, so ask the insurer rather than assume. If the child does not qualify for public insurance, commercial insurance for foreigners that meets the Act's requirements is needed. See how Czech health insurance works for foreigners and public health insurance: who pays and when . Once the child is insured, register with a paediatrician ( praktický lékař pro děti a dorost ), who will also handle the vaccination schedule and school health forms. Our guide to registering with a GP describes the process for adults, which is similar. Getting a child ready, in order Confirm the child's track Czech parent, EU parent or non-EU sponsor: the track decides the documents. Collect the child's documents abroad Birth certificate, passport and, where relevant, the other parent's consent or a court order, with apostilles and translations. Arrange accommodation and insurance A tenancy that covers the whole family and a policy that satisfies the Ministry. File the family permit Usually at a Czech embassy; track the waiting period and the sponsor's conditions. Register the address and the school After arrival, report the address and begin enrolment. Compulsory school Schooling in Czechia is compulsory for nine years, starting on 1 September after the child turns six. Children can start a year later in some cases by deferral, and some start earlier. The last year of pre-school ( mateřská škola ) before primary school is also compulsory, from the September after the child turns five, and free in public kindergartens; it applies to foreign children staying more than 90 days. Primary enrolment ( zápis ) takes place in April, and kindergarten applications are handled in a separate spring window (as of 2026; check the school and the district office). The Education Act (Act No. 561/2004 Coll.) gives children of foreigners access to primary and secondary school on the same terms as Czech children where the family stays in the country on a basis the law lists, which includes children of EU citizens and children of non-EU foreigners with lawful residence. Applicants do not have to speak Czech to enrol. Schools may offer extra Czech lessons and preparatory classes for pupils who need them, though the provision differs by school and municipality. In Prague, state primary schools are assigned by catchment area, and the school you are entitled to depends on your registered address. That makes the address registration an early priority. Read our guide to Prague school catchments , and for the address duty see registering your address . If you are still planning the move, the pre-departure checklist lists which school papers to bring. Choosing a school type Feature State school International or private school Language of teaching Czech, with support for newcomers in some schools Often English or another language Place assigned by Catchment area for primary schools Application to the school Fees Free tuition Fees set by the school Fit for Families staying long-term Families expecting to move on or wanting a foreign curriculum A general comparison; details vary by school. Check each school and the district office. Choosing between state and international schools State schools are free, taught in Czech and, for a child who will stay, the quickest route to integration. International and private schools teach in English or another language, charge fees and usually have their own admissions process; they suit families who expect to move on or who want a foreign curriculum. Hybrid arrangements exist, such as bilingual sections. A hypothetical family with two working parents with a six-year-old who plans to stay five years might choose a state school with Czech support and add English tutoring; a family expecting to leave in two years might choose an international school. Neither is better in general. Visit schools and ask specific questions: how many foreign pupils they have, what Czech support is offered, what happens in the first term, and how teachers communicate with parents who do not speak Czech. Do not rely on a list; programmes change. After the permit: what to keep up Children's permits need renewing like adults': see how to renew a Czech residence permit . Report address changes, keep insurance current and tell the Ministry about changes in the family's circumstances. A child who turns 18 stops being a minor under the family track and needs a new basis of stay, so plan a year before the birthday and ask the Ministry what the options are, including study. Frequently asked questions At what age does school start in Czechia? Compulsory schooling begins on 1 September after the child turns six, with a compulsory final year of pre-school before that. Does my child need to speak Czech to enrol? No. Children of foreigners with lawful residence have access to education on the same terms as Czech children, and many schools offer Czech support. How is a child insured? It depends on the family's status. Ask the health insurer whether the child qualifies for the public system; otherwise commercial insurance is needed. What if my child is born in Czechia? The baby needs a residence basis, which the parents must apply for within the period set in the Foreigners Act, commonly 60 days. Check the deadline with MV/OAMP.
